requests_have_timeout (SEC-013): fits. Used, with a param_required rule added because the template's param_bound alone passes an omitted timeout at its 10s default.
tls_verification_on (SEC-011): not asked for; the ask is timeout and error handling.

rules.covers: every external call sits in a try block so a vendor failure reaches error handling
every external HTTP call writes its own timeout (added so an omitted timeout does not pass on the 10s default)
no external HTTP call waits longer than 30 seconds, so one slow vendor cannot stall the app

ask_parts_not_covered.part: the catch block actually handles the failure (fallback, error response, logging)
timeouts on MCP and external database calls
ask_parts_not_covered.why: no check exists; those statements take no timeout parameter

ask_parts_not_covered.part: the app actually stops hanging when a vendor goes down, at run time
ask_parts_not_covered.why: needs runtime/org process; policies read stored definitions only

whether the 30-second ceiling is the right number for each vendor

assumptions: The ask 'any external API call' means every outbound statement the LOG-010 limits text names: api.request, stream.from_request, webflow.request, ai.external.mcp.*, db.external.*.direct_query.
The 30-second ceiling from the SEC-013 template is acceptable for the customer; the ask did not give a number.
Enforcement stays policy-only: existing call sites are reported, not edited, because changing payment and refund failure paths is a customer decision.
Policies are advisory, per the skill's default for new policies, since the customer asked for a policy and not for blocking.
confusions: The LOG-010 limit text says to add ai.external.mcp.* and db.external.*.direct_query to cover every outbound call, but statement.containment takes no wildcards. I had to infer exact names (db.external.<engine>.direct_query, ai.external.mcp.tool.run/list, server_details) from the catalogue's text. A list of exact external statement names in the templates doc would remove the guess.

SEC-013's template rule (param_bound, max 30) passes an omitted timeout at its 10s default. The customer's words were 'has a timeout set', which the template does not require. I added param_required; the template doc does not suggest pairing the two.
xano policy parse's pretty-print omits severity and tags, while -o json shows them. Easy to misread as dropped fields.
Running xano workspace push -d ./workspace from inside the workspace folder silently reports 'No changes to push' rather than an error about the path. Easy to misread as a clean dry run.

The skill says a template's rules should be used as written and only the asked-for part changed, but widening a template's statement list is a change to the template's coverage. I did it because the ask said 'any external API call'; the doc does not say whether that is an allowed change.
wished_for: An exact list of external-call statement names (api.request, stream.from_request, webflow.request, ai.external.mcp.*, db.external.*.direct_query) in the templates doc, marked as which ones take a timeout.
A recipe for external-call resilience that pairs timeout (explicit, bounded) and try_catch around each call, with the note that param_bound alone passes defaults.
A check or note on whether a catch block is non-empty or does something; LOG-010 passes an empty catch.
A way to see findings for the draft policies before pushing without running evaluate, or a note that dry-run does not evaluate them.
parse_errors_seen: ENOENT: relative path 'workspace/policies/SEC-013.xs' after my shell cwd moved into workspace (my path mistake, not a policy error)
dry_run_problems_seen: First dry run from inside workspace/ reported 'No changes to push' because -d ./workspace resolved to the wrong folder; re-ran from project root and got policy +2 created.
why_confidence: The two policies parse and dry-run clean, and they check the two things the ask names: each external call sits in a try_catch, and each HTTP call sets a timeout no longer than 30s. Confidence is only medium because the try_catch check does not read the catch block, MCP and database calls cannot be given a timeout, retry loops are not checked, and the expected findings come from reading the code, not from a policy evaluate. Nine existing call sites will be flagged; the code itself is unchanged.
